phonemes.desc: Slender (palatalized) dental nasal [n̠ʲ] — the tongue arched toward the hard palate, close to the 'ny' of 'new' spoken in an Irish accent; Irish n before i is always slender.
Long close [iː] releasing into a brief [ə]; Munster Irish sounds both beats — 'NEE-uv' — while the standard northern pronunciation draws them into one long syllable, 'NEEV'.
The lenited m of Irish spelling, sounded as broad [vˠ] — a soft 'v' closing the name; the h writes the lenition and is never an 'h' sound.

pronunciation.approximation: 'NEE-uv' (Munster) or 'NEEV' (standard) — the weight on the long 'ee', the final mh a soft v; never 'nee-AM' and never an English h.

kin.label: Old Irish
kin.form: Níam — the medieval spelling, the síneadh fada marking the long vowel; beside the common noun niam, 'lustre, brilliance'.

kin.label: The name as word
kin.form: niam (eDIL s.v. 1 niam), 'lustre, brilliance, radiance' — the name is the abstract noun made personal: 'the radiant one'.

kin.label: Other bearers
kin.form: Niamh, wife of Conall Cernach of the Ulster Cycle — the name was a stock of beauty, not unique to the Otherworld rider.

kin.label: Modern Irish
kin.form: Niamh — among the most popular Irish girls' names of the modern era, the unbroken living form.

pronunciation.note: Niamh is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the canonical modern Irish spelling is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The medieval spelling Níam carries a síneadh fada, but the name's standard modern form writes none, and the mh digraph is lenition written in plain Latin letters. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input.

domains.title: Beauty, Otherworld
domains.subtitle: The Golden-Haired Rider of Tír na nÓg
domains.lead: Niamh Chinn Óir — Niamh of the Golden Hair — is the bright daughter of the king of Tír na nÓg who rides out of the western sea on a white horse to claim the last great poet of the Fianna. She carries [[oisin|Oisín]] over the waves to the Land of Youth, where three hundred years pass as a single season, and when longing for Ireland breaks him she lends him the horse again with one command: whatever he sees, he must not set foot on Irish soil.

cards.name: The White Horse
cards.desc: The steed from over the sea that carries Oisín to Tír na nÓg and home again; the lay leaves it unnamed — later tradition gives it Manannán's horse, Enbarr.

cards.name: The Golden Hair
cards.desc: Chinn Óir, 'of the Golden Head' — the epithet by which she names herself in the lay: the brightness of her name made visible.

cards.name: Tír na nÓg
cards.desc: 'The Land of the Young', the Irish Otherworld across the western sea — where age, sickness, and decay never come.

cards.name: The Slab of Stone
cards.desc: The flagstone Oisín stoops to lift in an Irish glen; the girth breaks, his foot touches home soil, and three hundred years fall on him at once.

symbols.name: The golden hair
symbols.meaning: Brightness made visible — the name Niamh, 'radiance', worn as the epithet Chinn Óir

symbols.name: The white horse
symbols.meaning: The Otherworld's transport, and the vehicle of the warning: cross the sea-road, but never touch the ground of home

symbols.name: The sea-crossing
symbols.meaning: The threshold between the mortal world and Tír na nÓg, ridden as if it were a road

symbols.name: The three hundred years
symbols.meaning: Time suspended in the Land of Youth — the Otherworld's gift and its price, counted only when it is spent

symbols.name: The broken girth
symbols.meaning: The single touch of Irish soil that undoes the enchantment — mortality resumed in an instant

mythology.lead: Niamh's story survives as one tale told one way: the lay Laoi Oisín ar Thír na nÓg, 'The Lay of Oisín in the Land of Youth', ascribed to the eighteenth-century poet Mícheál Coimín and first printed with an English translation by the Ossianic Society in 1859. It is late, beloved, and complete — the fullest Otherworld courtship in Irish literature, and the story every retelling since has followed.

myths.tag: Laoi Oisín ar Thír na nÓg
myths.title: The Summons from over the Sea
myths.text:
Oisín, son of [[fionn|Fionn mac Cumhaill]] and last great poet of the Fianna, is with his people when a maiden none of them knows rides out of the west on a white horse. She names herself: Niamh Chinn Óir, Niamh of the Golden Hair, daughter of the king of Tír na nÓg. She has heard the fame of Oisín across the sea, she says, and she has come for his love — her praise of him rises above every man of the Fianna present.

Oisín answers that he has never seen her equal, gives her his word, and mounts the white horse behind her. It is the simplest bargain in the Fenian cycle: no riddle, no quest, no combat — only a beautiful stranger keeping her promise to carry him to the land where no one grows old, and a poet who has never once been able to refuse a story.

myths.tag: Laoi Oisín ar Thír na nÓg
myths.title: The Wonders on the Wave
myths.text:
The white horse rides the sea as if it were a road, and the crossing is the lay's strangest passage. Marvels pass them on the wave: a fawn coursed by a white hound with red ears; a maiden riding with a golden apple in her hand; a young rider in a crimson cloak hard behind her, a gold-hilted sword at his side. Oisín asks what these things mean, and the lay lets them pass unexplained — the Otherworld does not interpret itself for passengers.

The images are the old heraldry of the Irish síd — the red-eared hound, the golden fruit, the pursuit that never ends — set loose on the open sea. Between Ireland and Tír na nÓg there is no geography, only signs.

myths.tag: Laoi Oisín ar Thír na nÓg
myths.title: Three Hundred Years as a Dream
myths.text:
In the Land of Youth the king receives Oisín, and he and Niamh are made one. There is no age there and no decay; the days pass in music, hunting, and delight, and the reckoning of them slips away. Niamh bears Oisín three children, and at his asking they are named for the world he left: the sons Fionn and Oscar, for his father and his son, and the daughter Plúr na mBan — 'flower of women'.

Three hundred years go by, sweet as a single season. The lay's arithmetic is the whole point of the Otherworld: time in Tír na nÓg is not slower than mortal time — it simply does not accrue. Nothing is saved. Nothing is spent. And nothing, in the end, is enough to make a Fenian forget the Fianna.

myths.tag: Laoi Oisín ar Thír na nÓg
myths.title: The Warning and the Horse
myths.text:
Longing comes on Oisín at last: to see Ireland again, to look for his father Fionn and the remnant of the Fianna, to stand once more on the hills of his own country. Niamh does not refuse him. She gives him the white horse for the journey, and with it the command on which everything turns: ride where he will, look where he will — but he must not dismount, for if his foot touches the soil of Ireland he will never return to the Land of Youth.

The warning is the oldest law of the fairy-visit: the mortal may look back, but he may not re-enter. Niamh has kept him three hundred years from the thing she now names — time — and she sends him home wrapped in the only protection she has: a horse, and an instruction.

myths.tag: Laoi Oisín ar Thír na nÓg
myths.title: The Slab in the Glen
myths.text:
Ireland is changed past recognition. The Fianna are gone; their ramparts are green mounds; the people are small, and Christianity has come. In a glen of the south — the lay names Gleann an Smóil, the valley of the thrushes — Oisín comes upon a company of men straining to raise a great flagstone that any one man of the Fianna would have lifted alone. Leaning down from the saddle to help them, he puts his strength to the stone — and the saddle-girth breaks.

He falls, and his foot touches the soil of Ireland. In that instant the three hundred years land on him: the youth goes out of him, and he rises an old, withered, grey-haired man, while the white horse wheels away over the sea to Tír na nÓg without him. Niamh's warning was exact. The Land of Youth keeps its own; it does not give them back.

myths.title: The Old Man and the Saint
myths.text:
The lay ends where the medieval tradition had long ago stationed Oisín: at the door of St. Patrick. The Acallam na Senórach, the Colloquy of the Ancients composed around 1200, already framed its whole Fenian treasury this way — Oisín and Caílte, the last survivors of the Fianna, walking Ireland with Patrick and reciting its lore place by place. The Niamh episode itself belongs to the later lay tradition, not to the Acallam, but the ending is one: the pagan hero out of time, telling the golden age to the new faith, and refusing to the last to prefer heaven to the Fianna.

Niamh never appears again. She remains in Tír na nÓg with their children — Fionn, Oscar, and Plúr na mBan — on the far side of a sea that Oisín, earthbound and mortal again, will never cross. The white horse came home without a rider. The lay does not say she grieved; it does not need to.

lore.syncretism: Niamh belongs to the oldest company in Irish narrative: the Otherworld woman who comes for a mortal man. Echtrae Chonnlai gives the type its starkest form — a woman of the síd, visible only to Connla, throws him an apple that never diminishes and calls him to Mag Mell, until he leaps into her crystal ship and is seen no more. Immram Brain sends a woman from Emain with a silver branch to summon Bran across the sea to the Land of Women, where a year is no time at all — the same time-arithmetic as Oisín's three centuries. In Tochmarc Étaíne the direction reverses: [[midir|Midir]] of Brí Léith wins back [[etain|Étaín]] and the two fly from Tara as swans. The frame that late tradition gave Niamh herself is genealogical: she is made a daughter of [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]], lord of the sea-Otherworlds Emain Ablach and Mag Mell, whose Welsh cognate is [[manawydan|Manawydan fab Llŷr]] — the lay itself names her only as the daughter of Tír na nÓg's king, and the Manannán paternity is the tradition's own harmonization. Folklore comparison adds the international motif: the supernatural lapse of time in fairyland, the traveller who returns to find centuries gone, which Hartland made the type-case of his Science of Fairy Tales. The Welsh corpus preserves no Niamh; the nearest Brythonic resonances are [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]]'s unmatchable horse and the raid on [[annwn|Annwn]] in Preiddeu Annwn — kinship of motif, never of name.
lore.culturalLegacy: Niamh has the largest modern afterlife of any Irish Otherworld woman, and it runs through one poem. W. B. Yeats's The Wanderings of Oisin (1889) — his first major work and the foundation-poem of the Irish Literary Revival — took the lay's summons as its frame: Niamh calls Oisin away on the white horse, and three enchanted islands later he returns to a Christian Ireland and dies with the Fianna on his lips. Yeats's three islands are his own invention, but the wooer is the lay's, and through him Niamh became the world literature's type of the Celtic Otherworld bride. Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried the prose retelling to the same generation. In Ireland itself the name went the opposite way from mythology to the birth register: Niamh became one of the most popular Irish girls' names of the late twentieth century, so that the golden-haired rider is now, for most who bear the name, simply themselves. And Tír na nÓg has passed into the general vocabulary as the default name of the Celtic paradise — the land over the western sea where nobody grows old, reached only on a white horse, and only in her company.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Niamh is the name of a temptation, and the temptation is not what it first seems. She offers beauty, youth, and three hundred years without a wrinkle — and the story's verdict is that the offer is genuine. Tír na nÓg is no trap: the children are real, the delight is real, the warning she gives him is honest and exact. What the lay understands is that exemption from time is itself a kind of exile, and that a mortal carries his mortality inside him as homesickness. Oisín does not fall because the Otherworld failed him; he falls because Ireland is his, and a single touch of its soil outweighs three centuries of paradise.

Her name keeps the paradox in one syllable. Niamh — radiance, the shining thing — is the brightest name in the Fenian cycle, and she rides it out of the sea to the one man whose whole art was memory. Between them the lay poses the question it never answers: is the golden age the land across the water where nothing ages, or the lost Ireland of the Fianna that the old poet spends his last days reciting to a saint? Niamh holds one answer. Oisín holds the other. The white horse runs between them, and it does not wait.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in medieval Irish manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as Níam — Old and Middle Irish in Insular minuscule — beside the common noun niam, 'lustre, brilliance'; the canonical modern Irish spelling Niamh writes the lenited m with the digraph mh and drops the fada. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, predates the manuscript tradition, but no attestation of this name has ever been read on an ogham stone — the four hundred-odd stones mark graves and boundaries with men's names in formulaic genitives, and Ireland's pagan world left literature, not dedications. The modern form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — which fixes the name in Tier 2. Because it is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: niamh.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Niamh is an entirely textual figure: no ogham stone names her, no votive deposit invokes her, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. Her tale has an exact documentary trail: the Laoi Oisín ar Thír na nÓg, ascribed to the eighteenth-century Clare poet Mícheál Coimín, survives in the Irish paper-manuscript tradition and reached print in the Transactions of the Ossianic Society (vol. 4, 1859), the learned society that did for the Fenian lays what Grimm did for the folktale. The medieval frame into which the lay fits its ending — Oisín and Caílte reciting Ireland to St. Patrick — is preserved in the Acallam na Senórach, whose great witness is the fifteenth-century Book of Lismore, with Laud Misc. 610 among its sister codices. Her Otherworld has no fixed address, and that is its nature: unlike the Dagda's Brú na Bóinne, where Newgrange gives myth a monument, Tír na nÓg was never mapped onto any real island — the material record of Niamh is the manuscript tradition itself, and the unbroken popularity of her name.
